pages.p:
So far your code ran every line, top to bottom. With **if** the program can decide. After «if» you write a **condition** in round brackets. A condition is a question with the answer true or false, like «temperature > 25».

The code inside the curly braces «{ }» runs only when the condition is true.
pages.tip: If the condition were false, only «Done» would print. The last line is outside the braces, so it always runs.

pages.p: Add **else** to say what to do when the condition is false. Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both and never neither.
pages.tip: «else» has no condition of its own. It simply means "in every other case".

pages.h: else if: more than two choices
pages.p: Sometimes there are three or more choices. Put **else if** (with its own condition) between «if» and «else». JavaScript checks from the top. The **first** true condition wins, and all the rest are skipped.

Because the first true condition wins, the order of your checks is important. Here the score is 95, and we wanted «Top». But «95 >= 50» is true, so the first block runs and the second is never reached.
pages.tip: Put the strictest condition first (90 before 50).

pages.p: You met «&&» (and), «||» (or) and «!» (not) in the last unit. Conditions are where they shine. «&&» needs both sides true. «||» needs at least one side true.
pages.tip: Write each comparison in full. «day === "Sat" || "Sun"» does not work the way it looks.

pages.p: In a function, «return» ends the function straight away. So you can return early from inside an «if». Code after a returned line never runs. The last «return» catches every case the «if» blocks did not.

A condition does not have to be a comparison. JavaScript can treat **any** value as true or false. The values that count as **falsy** are: «false», «0», «""» (empty text), «null», «undefined» and «NaN». Everything else is **truthy**, even the text «"0"».
pages.o:
Please type a name
Text with a zero is truthy
pages.tip: Handy: «if (name)» means "if name is not empty".

pages.p:
Remember «%» gives the remainder. It makes great conditions. A number is even when «n % 2 === 0». It is a multiple of 5 when «n % 5 === 0».

Beware of a classic slip: «=» stores a value, «===» compares. Inside an «if», you almost always want «===».

For a simple two-way choice there is a short form: «condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse». It is called the **ternary operator** because it has three parts. It is an expression, so it gives you a value you can store.
The ternary operator is perfect after «return», when each branch is a single value. Use a normal «if» when the branches need several lines. Short and clear beats clever.
When you compare one value against many exact options, **switch** is tidy. Each «case» is an option. «break» leaves the switch. «default» runs when no case matches. «switch» compares with «===».
Without «break», JavaScript **falls through**: it also runs the code of the next case. Sometimes that is useful. Stacking cases with no code between them lets several values share one result.
pages.tip: Forgetting «break» is the most common switch bug.

hand.why: 5 > 3 is true, so only the if block runs. The last line is outside, so it always runs.

hand.q: When does the else block run?
hand.ans: When the if condition is false
wrong: Every time, right after the if block
When the if condition is true
Only when the program has an error
hand.why: else is the "otherwise" path: it runs only if the condition was false.
85 is not at least 90, but it is at least 80. That is the first true condition, so the rest are skipped, even though 85 >= 70 is true too.

hand.q: Complete the condition so that exactly 18 counts as an adult.
hand.why: «>=» means greater than or equal, so 18 passes. Plain «>» would leave 18 out.

hand.q: Put the lines in order to print even or odd.
hand.why: The variable comes first, then the if with its condition, then the else block, and the closing brace last.

hand.q: Which condition is true when x is from 1 to 10, including 1 and 10?
hand.why: Both limits must hold, so use «&&». «||» would be true for every number, and «>» / «<» would leave out 1 and 10.
«a && b» is false, because b is false. «a || b» is true, because a is true. So the second block runs.
The shape is «condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse». The «?» comes right after the condition.
5 > 3 is true, so the first ternary gives «yes». 2 > 3 is false, so the second gives «no».

hand.q: What happens if you forget break at the end of a case?
hand.ans: The next case's code runs as well
wrong: The switch starts again from the top
hand.why: Without «break», execution falls through into the following case, running its lines too.
n is 2, so «case 2» matches, prints «two», and «break» leaves the switch before «default».
Empty text is falsy, so the condition counts as false and the else block runs.

hand.q: Which word starts the block that runs when no case matches?
hand.why: «default:» is the catch-all of a switch, like «else» in an if.

hand.q: Put the lines in order so the program prints "Adult".
hand.why: The variable must exist first, then the ternary uses it to choose a word, and only then can you print the result.

hard.why: These are two separate «if» statements, not an else-if chain. Both conditions are true, so both blocks run, each on its own line.
The «else» belongs only to the second «if». The first if prints A, and then the second if (5 > 4) prints B.

hard.q: Which of these values is truthy?
hard.why: Only the number 0, empty text, null, undefined, NaN and false are falsy. Any non-empty text, even «"0"», is truthy.
«case 2» matches and prints b. It has no «break», so it falls into «case 3», prints c, and that «break» stops everything.
«a > b» is false, so the first ternary gives b, which is 9. 4 is even, so the second gives «even».
20 > 10, so «return "big"» ends the function at once. The «checking» line is never reached.

hard.q: Why is this condition always true?
hard.ans: 2 is truthy on its own, so the || is always true
wrong: It is true only when x is 2
hard.why: «x === 1 || 2» means «(x === 1) || 2». The «2» alone is truthy. You must write «x === 1 || x === 2».
The limits use «<», so 13 is already an adult and 65 is already a senior. Check the edges carefully.
1900 divides by 4 and 100 but not 400, so false. 2000 divides by 400, so true. 2024 divides by 4 but not 100, so true.

hard.q: Add the line so that only «Good» is printed.
hard.why: Without a «break», «Good» would be followed by «Try again». «break» stops the switch after the shared block.

items.symptom: It prints Exactly 18 even though age is 20.
items.why: A single «=» stores 18 into age, and 18 is truthy. To compare, use «===».

items.symptom: A score of exactly 90 prints Pass, but it should print Excellent.
items.why: «>» leaves out 90 itself. The edge value needs «>=».

items.symptom: The program crashes with a SyntaxError before printing anything.
items.why: The condition of an «if» must be inside round brackets.

items.symptom: Someone with no ID is let in, but the rule says both are needed.
items.why: «||» needs only one true side. When both things are required, use «&&».

items.symptom: A SyntaxError appears and nothing is printed.
items.why: «default» needs a colon, just like each «case».

items.symptom: It prints No name even though name is "Sam".
items.why: The text «"Sam"» is not strictly equal to «true», even though it is truthy. Use «if (name)» to test for non-empty text.

project.title: Rock Paper Scissors Referee
project.brief:
Write a function «rps» that decides a round of rock paper scissors. It gets two inputs, «a» and «b», each one of the texts «"rock"», «"paper"» or «"scissors"».

Return «"tie"» if they are the same. Return «"first"» if «a» wins and «"second"» if «b» wins. Rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, paper beats rock.

Example: «rps("rock", "scissors")» returns «"first"».
